summary: One setting: its name and description on the left, the control on the right — and the control named and described by them automatically.
useWhen: a settings or preferences panel, one row per setting
a control whose meaning needs a sentence of explanation beside it

useInstead.when: it is a form field with its own visible label above it
useInstead.why: Input, Select and the pickers carry their own label and description; a SettingRow around them names the field twice

useInstead.when: a group of options answers one question
useInstead.why: the group has its own label; put the RadioGroup under a heading rather than in a row

children.note: an element is cloned with aria-labelledby and aria-describedby pointing at the row's text; a function receives the ids instead, for a control that needs them somewhere else

guarantees: an element child with no text of its own — a Toggle, a Checkbox with no label — is named by the row's label and described by its description, so it is announced as "Weekly digest, switch, off" plus what it does, not "switch, off"
a child with its own text — a Button — keeps that text as its name (WCAG 2.5.3), and the row's label and description are attached as its description instead
an aria-labelledby or aria-describedby the caller passes explicitly is kept, never overwritten
it stacks by its own width, so it reads the same in a page and in a narrow drawer
requires: one control per row — the ids name one element
notes: The label is text, not a <label>, because the control may be a Button; a <label> pointing at a button is invalid.

antiPatterns.dont: a Toggle or Checkbox with its own visible label inside a SettingRow
antiPatterns.why: the control then names itself, the row's label becomes a description, and the setting's name is shown twice

antiPatterns.dont: a Checkbox row that saves immediately
antiPatterns.why: Toggle is immediate and Checkbox is saved with a submit — the SettingsPanel pattern's first rule
